collections.title: Signals From the Ice
collections.dek: Stations, bases and recordings from both polar regions.

collections.title: The Numbers Station Archive
collections.dek: Coded voices and military channels that never explain themselves.

collections.title: The World's Maritime Frequencies
collections.dek: Forecasts, coast stations and one real distress call.

collections.title: Broadcasts Beyond Midnight
collections.dek: Recordings from the small hours and the turn of the year.

collections.title: Sounds From the Earth's Infrastructure
collections.dek: Time signals, aviation weather and navigation tones.

collections.title: The Planet's Own Radio
collections.dek: Natural very-low-frequency signals and one from deep space.

collections.title: Voices Across the Line
collections.dek: Broadcasts across closed borders in Asia.

collections.title: Transmission Art
collections.dek: Stations that treat radio itself as the medium.

sources.title: BBC Radio 4
sources.blurb: The home of the Shipping Forecast, the Met Office bulletin read to the seas around the British Isles since the 1920s. The late edition at 00:48 UK time is preceded by 'Sailing By' and carries the full set of coastal station reports.
sources.hear: Most of the day it is speech radio. At 00:48 and 05:20 UK time a single voice reads gale warnings and sea areas in fixed order, from Viking round to Southeast Iceland.

sources.title: BBC World Service
sources.blurb: The international service that shortwave listeners have tuned to for nearly a century, now reaching most of its audience online and by relay. Its English stream runs around the clock from Broadcasting House.
sources.hear: Rolling international news and documentary, with the hourly pips and bulletins that once crossed oceans on shortwave.

sources.title: NOAA Weather Radio KEC49
sources.blurb: One of more than a thousand VHF transmitters of NOAA Weather Radio, broadcasting from a Bay Area summit for the Monterey forecast office. A volunteer receiver picks it off the air and puts it online.
sources.hear: A synthesised voice cycling through forecasts, observations and marine conditions on a loop that updates as the forecasters do. Alert tones interrupt it when warnings are issued.

sources.title: NOAA Weather Radio WWG24
sources.blurb: A NOAA Weather Radio transmitter its volunteer relay lists as serving the Puget Sound marine area. These broadcasts are a working tool for ferries, tugs and small craft in the sound.
sources.hear: Automated readings of wind, wave and visibility for the inland waters, repeated on a loop.

sources.title: CBC North — Iqaluit
sources.blurb: The public broadcaster's service for Canada's far north, heard from the capital of Nunavut on Baffin Island. Programming moves between English and Inuktitut.
sources.hear: Regional news, community notices and music from a town of a few thousand people on Frobisher Bay.

sources.title: NRK Sápmi
sources.blurb: Norway's Sámi-language public radio, based above the Arctic Circle in Finnmark. It serves the Indigenous people of northern Scandinavia in their own languages.
sources.hear: News and talk in Northern Sámi, with joik and Sámi popular music between programmes.

sources.title: Yle Sámi Radio
sources.blurb: Finland's Sámi public service, broadcasting from Lapland. It is one of very few places on air where several of the endangered Sámi languages are spoken daily.
sources.hear: Sámi-language news, talk and music from the far north of Finland.

sources.title: BFBS Falklands
sources.blurb: The forces broadcaster for the British garrison in the South Atlantic, one of the most remote postings in the armed forces. It also serves the islands' civilian population.
sources.hear: Presenter-led music and local announcements for a military community thousands of miles from home.

sources.title: BFBS Gurkha Radio
sources.blurb: A British military station that first went on air in 1952 inside a Gurkha recruiting camp at Dharan in eastern Nepal. It links Nepali soldiers in the British Army with their families.
sources.hear: Nepali music and news from Kathmandu, carried to Gurkha units in the UK and wherever they are deployed.

sources.title: Vatican Radio — English
sources.blurb: The broadcaster of the world's smallest state, founded in 1931 with help from Guglielmo Marconi. It runs services in dozens of languages from inside the Vatican walls.
sources.hear: The English service: news from the Holy See, liturgy and sacred music.

sources.title: Radio Prague International
sources.blurb: Czech Radio's external service, once a Cold War shortwave voice and now carried online. Its schedule rotates through several languages across the day.
sources.hear: Short magazine programmes about Czech life in English, German, French, Spanish and Russian, depending on the hour.

sources.title: WGXC 90.7 — Wave Farm
sources.blurb: A full-power community station in the Upper Hudson Valley run by Wave Farm, an arts organisation built around transmission art. It mixes local information with radio as an artistic medium.
sources.hear: Anything from county news to commissioned radio art and sound experiments.

sources.title: Standing Wave Radio
sources.blurb: Wave Farm's channel for experimental sound and transmission art, also radiated on 1620 kHz AM across its 29-acre art park. Artists' installations on the site feed it directly.
sources.hear: Long-form sound works and site installations. Some hours are close to silence; that is part of the programme.

sources.title: Resonance Extra
sources.blurb: The round-the-clock experimental sister of London's Resonance 104.4 FM, a station run by artists since 2002.
sources.hear: Sound art, field recording, improvised music and radio works rarely heard elsewhere.

sources.title: Cashmere Radio
sources.blurb: A non-commercial experimental station broadcasting from a Berlin studio, run by its community of resident hosts.
sources.hear: Ambient, drone, improvisation and spoken works, scheduled by human hosts rather than an algorithm.

sources.title: Radio WORM
sources.blurb: The radio arm of WORM, a Rotterdam institution for avant-garde and DIY culture.
sources.hear: Interviews, mixes and sound art from the city's experimental scene.

sources.title: Radio Is a Foreign Country
sources.blurb: A non-profit station built on cut-ups of international AM, FM and shortwave broadcasts and obscure regional folk and pop. It sounds like someone else's dial at three in the morning.
sources.hear: Field-taped radio from far-off places, interval tunes and old regional records, stitched together without commentary.

sources.title: MorseOps — 20 WPM
sources.blurb: A continuous Morse practice channel from MorseOps, a CW training site built by a licensed amateur, KI7NTK. Morse remains a living mode on the amateur bands.
sources.hear: Machine-sent Morse at 20 words per minute, the speed many operators work at on the air.

sources.title: KNR — Kalaallit Nunaata Radioa
sources.blurb: Greenland's national public broadcaster, on air from Nuuk since 1958 and known by its Greenlandic name since 1981. It serves a country of scattered towns with no roads between them, mostly in Kalaallisut, the Greenlandic language.
sources.hear: Greenlandic news and talk with some Danish, and music between programmes. Its own programming runs from 07:00 to 23:00 Nuuk time.

sources.title: SR Sápmi
sources.blurb: Sveriges Radio's Sámi channel, based in Kiruna with bureaus across northern Sweden and Norway. It covers the Sámi, Sápmi and other Indigenous peoples, with Northern Sámi as the usual base language for news.
sources.hear: Ođđasat, the shared Nordic Sámi news, plus talk and music. With NRK Sápmi and Yle Sámi it completes the Sámi public radio of all three Nordic countries.

sources.title: Orcasound Lab hydrophone
sources.geoNote: Hydrophone off the west side of San Juan Island; position approximate.
sources.credit: Orcasound cooperative, hosted by Beam Reach
sources.blurb: A live underwater microphone in the summer habitat of the endangered Southern Resident killer whales, running since 2002. Volunteers and detection software listen around the clock and raise the alarm when whales are heard.
sources.hear: Mostly the sea: waves, the drone of ships in the shipping lane and boats along the shore. Now and then, orca calls, clicks or humpback song.

sources.title: The Lincolnshire Poacher
sources.geoNote: Location widely attributed, never officially confirmed.
sources.blurb: The most famous numbers station of all, widely attributed to British intelligence. It opened with bars of the English folk song it is named after, then read groups of five numbers in a clipped female voice. It went silent in 2008.
sources.hear: Bars of 'The Lincolnshire Poacher' played on a loop, then numbers. The station never identified itself.

sources.title: The Swedish Rhapsody
sources.blurb: Named after its music-box interval melody, a fragment of Hugo Alfvén's Swedish Rhapsody No. 1. Listeners have long attributed it to Polish intelligence.
sources.hear: A tinny music box, then a young girl's voice, or a recording of one, reading numbers in German. Many listeners find it the most unsettling recording on the Conet set.

sources.title: HM01 — Cuban numbers station
sources.geoNote: Attributed to Cuban intelligence by listeners and in court cases; position approximate.
sources.blurb: Still heard regularly when this was recorded in 2013, HM01 mixes a Spanish-speaking female voice with bursts of digital data, and is attributed to Cuba's intelligence service.
sources.hear: A Spanish number count interleaved with warbling data bursts, recorded at 10:00 UTC on 5,855 kHz.

sources.title: UVB-76 — 'The Buzzer'
sources.geoNote: Transmitter site has moved over the years; position shown is approximate.
sources.credit: Pedro Calhau via the Shortwave Radio Audio Archive
sources.blurb: A Russian military channel on 4625 kHz that has sent a short, harsh buzz day and night for decades. Occasionally the buzz stops and a voice reads a coded message.
sources.hear: The buzz itself, captured in 2018 from the Netherlands through the University of Twente's web receiver.

sources.title: Emergency Action Message — HFGCS
sources.geoNote: Marker shows where it was received; HFGCS transmits from sites worldwide.
sources.credit: John Lutz via the Shortwave Radio Audio Archive
sources.blurb: The US Air Force's High Frequency Global Communications System passes encrypted Emergency Action Messages to aircraft, ground stations and some ships. Their meaning is classified; listeners log them by the hundred.
sources.hear: An operator reading a long string of phonetic letters and numbers on 8,992 kHz, just before 05:00 UTC.

sources.title: American Forces Antarctic Network
sources.credit: Tony King via the Shortwave Radio Audio Archive
sources.blurb: The armed forces radio station for McMurdo, the largest base in Antarctica. This rare 1980s catch on single sideband was made from New Zealand.
sources.hear: A forces radio programme from the bottom of the world, faint and wavering across the Southern Ocean.

sources.title: CHU — Canada's time signal
sources.blurb: Canada's official shortwave time station, broadcasting from Ottawa at 10 kW. Every minute it announces the time in English and French.
sources.hear: Ticks each second and a bilingual voice announcement, heard here from Sydney, Australia.

sources.title: WWVH — Jane Barbe's voice
sources.credit: Myke Dodge Weiskopf via the Shortwave Radio Audio Archive
sources.blurb: NIST's Pacific time station as it sounded in the 1980s, found on an undated cassette at the WWVH site in 2015. The voice is Jane Barbe, also known as the voice of countless US telephone recordings.
sources.hear: Second ticks and the station identification around 23:59 UTC, the turn of the day in Coordinated Universal Time.

sources.title: Shannon VOLMET
sources.credit: Stewart Killeen via the Shortwave Radio Audio Archive
sources.blurb: VOLMET is aviation's round-the-clock weather broadcast for aircraft in flight. Shannon's serves transatlantic crews in the Shanwick oceanic area of the north-east Atlantic.
sources.hear: A measured voice reading SIGMET warnings and airport conditions across Europe, recorded in Dublin.

sources.title: New York & Gander VOLMET, 1975
sources.blurb: Two transatlantic weather broadcasts caught on the Pacific coast of Canada in 1975, when VOLMET still went out in AM. They remain on air today in single sideband.
sources.hear: New York and then Gander reading airport weather, a routine message heard thousands of miles from its intended crews.

sources.title: The Shipping Forecast, off air
sources.credit: Richard Langley via the Shortwave Radio Audio Archive
sources.blurb: The late Shipping Forecast caught on longwave from the 500 kW Droitwich transmitter, the way it was meant to be heard at sea.
sources.hear: 'Sailing By', the forecast, the national anthem closing Radio 4's day, and the six pips, under a little static.

sources.title: Bollettino del Mare, 1977
sources.credit: Andrea Borgnino via the Shortwave Radio Audio Archive
sources.blurb: Italy's equivalent of the Shipping Forecast, in a 1977 studio recording from RAI.
sources.hear: Sea states and winds for the Mediterranean, read with the cadence of a litany.

sources.title: US Coast Guard NMC, 2003
sources.credit: Bruce Atchison via the Shortwave Radio Audio Archive
sources.blurb: NMC is the Coast Guard's Pacific communications station, broadcasting high-seas weather and safety messages to ships. The recordist logged it somewhere around 8 MHz.
sources.hear: A marine safety broadcast for vessels far out in the Pacific.

sources.title: Night of Nights, 2015
sources.credit: Eric Christensen via the Shortwave Radio Audio Archive
sources.blurb: Every July, former coast stations return to the air in Morse to mark the end of commercial maritime telegraphy in the US. This capture includes NMC and WLO.
sources.hear: Several shore stations sending Morse at once, heard from Chesapeake Beach, Maryland.

sources.title: SOS — ms Prinsendam, 1980
sources.credit: USCG Kodiak original; digitised by David J. Ring Jr., N1EA
sources.blurb: The cruise ship Prinsendam caught fire in the Gulf of Alaska. Its chief radio officer worked Coast Guard station Kodiak, which advised him to send an SOS preceded by the auto-alarm so it would wake sleeping operators on nearby ships. Everyone aboard was rescued.
sources.hear: A genuine distress call in Morse, kept by the Coast Guard station that received it.

sources.title: LRA36 — Radio Nacional Arcángel San Gabriel
sources.credit: Dan Greenall via the Shortwave Radio Audio Archive
sources.blurb: Argentina's radio station on the Antarctic Peninsula, one of the hardest catches on the shortwave dial. Its 10 kW signal was usually buried in noise when it reached the northern hemisphere.
sources.hear: Spanish announcements with the station ID, frequency and power, logged after many attempts in Ontario.

sources.title: BBC Antarctic Midwinter Broadcast, 2023
sources.geoNote: Marker shows the audience; the broadcast originates in London.
sources.blurb: Once a year on the winter solstice, the BBC World Service sends a half-hour of shortwave to the British Antarctic Survey staff wintering in the dark. In 2023 there were 37 of them.
sources.hear: Messages from families and friends, music requests and a test tone before the transmitter opens.

sources.title: Ham contact with Palmer Station, 1974
sources.credit: Recorded by W2PVF; shared by Bill Hemphill, WD9EQD, via the Shortwave Radio Audio Archive
sources.blurb: A New Jersey radio amateur talking to the US research base at Palmer Station, taped in 1974 and found decades later at an estate sale.
sources.hear: Two operators chatting across the hemispheres, joined mid-conversation.

sources.title: Storm at Taubanesentralen
sources.blurb: The derelict hub of the cable cars that once carried coal from Longyearbyen's mines, recorded on a stormy night with contact microphones on the structure.
sources.hear: The building itself singing in the wind: groans, rattles and resonance from steel and timber.

sources.title: Pyramiden, the ghost town
sources.blurb: A Soviet mining town abandoned in 1998 and left much as it was. The recordist was confined to the group because of polar bears, so she taped outside the hotel bar.
sources.hear: Thousands of kittiwakes that have taken over one of the empty buildings.

sources.title: Radio Pyongyang, 1975
sources.blurb: North Korea's English-language propaganda at the height of the Cold War, taped on the west coast of Canada from a cassette archive reopened 46 years later.
sources.hear: Martial music and long tributes to the leadership, delivered in formal English.

sources.title: Voice of Korea, 2024
sources.credit: Anthony Messina via the Shortwave Radio Audio Archive
sources.blurb: The same station half a century on, now called Voice of Korea and still broadcasting on shortwave. These recent captures were made through a web receiver in Japan.
sources.hear: A collection of early-2024 English broadcasts, little changed in tone from the 1970s.

sources.title: KCBS Sinuiju
sources.credit: Paul Walker via the Shortwave Radio Audio Archive
sources.blurb: North Korea's domestic Korean Central Broadcasting Station, relayed on 250 kW medium wave from the Chinese border and heard 3,500 miles away in McGrath, Alaska.
sources.hear: Instrumental North Korean music holding up for more than six minutes across the Bering region.

sources.title: Furusato no Kaze
sources.geoNote: Marker shows the transmitter; the programme is made in Japan and aimed at North Korea.
sources.blurb: 'Hometown Wind', a Japanese government programme meant for Japanese citizens abducted by North Korea who may still be alive there. It goes out by shortwave because almost nothing else gets in.
sources.hear: Gentle Japanese speech and music for listeners who may never be able to reply, heard in London from a 100 kW transmitter in Palau.

sources.title: Tibet People's Broadcasting Station
sources.credit: Brett Saylor via the Shortwave Radio Audio Archive
sources.blurb: The regional broadcaster of Lhasa on the 60-metre tropical band, heard from Pennsylvania at the top of the hour.
sources.hear: Time pips and a station identification that includes English.

sources.title: Voice of Mongolia
sources.blurb: Mongolia's external service broadcasting in English to South-East Asia at 250 kW from Khonkhor, outside Ulaanbaatar.
sources.hear: Interval signal, sign-on, news, a commentary on climate change in Mongolia, music and sign-off, heard in Sydney.

sources.title: France Inter longwave signs off
sources.blurb: The last hour of France Inter on longwave, broadcast on New Year's Eve 2016 from the 2,000 kW Allouis transmitter near Bourges.
sources.hear: The 23:00 CET time tones, a news bulletin and an end-of-year music show, until the frequency falls silent.

sources.title: Radio Australia rings in 2000
sources.blurb: Part of a round-the-world project to record broadcasters as each crossed into the year 2000, captured on a ham transceiver and a long wire strung across a relative's garden.
sources.hear: Radio Australia's millennium midnight as it reached a listener on the far side of the world.

sources.title: Shortwave IDs & interval signals, 1991
sources.geoNote: Marker shows where it was recorded.
sources.credit: Frank via the Shortwave Radio Audio Archive
sources.blurb: A teenage listener's cassette from just after German reunification, when former East German broadcasters were changing names. It gathers station IDs, interval signals, European pirates and a few numbers stations.
sources.hear: Side one: the identifying melodies that state broadcasters played before going on air.

sources.title: KGO, minutes after Loma Prieta
sources.blurb: At 5:04 pm on 17 October 1989 a magnitude 6.9 earthquake hit northern California during the World Series. A listener who had been watching the game turned to KGO San Francisco on 810 kHz.
sources.hear: Breaking news as it happened: live reports and callers in the first confused hour after the quake.

sources.title: Dawn chorus, Alberta
sources.credit: Stephen P. McGreevy, Auroral Chorus II
sources.blurb: 'Dawn chorus' here means a radio phenomenon: electrons in Earth's magnetosphere radiate rising tones at very low frequency, often around local dawn. A receiver and a wire antenna turn them straight into sound.
sources.hear: A twittering swarm of rising notes, uncannily like birdsong, recorded in stereo in Alberta.

sources.title: Whistlers over Battersea Park
sources.credit: Stephen P. McGreevy, Auroral Chorus II
sources.blurb: A whistler starts as the radio crash of a lightning stroke, often in the opposite hemisphere, then travels along Earth's magnetic field and arrives stretched into a falling tone. These were caught on football pitches in central London.
sources.hear: Descending whistles over the crackle of distant lightning, an evening in May 1996.

sources.title: Strong chorus, Kenai Peninsula
sources.credit: Stephen P. McGreevy, Auroral Chorus II
sources.blurb: Chorus is strongest at high latitudes, under the auroral zone. This was recorded by a lake on Alaska's Kenai Peninsula.
sources.hear: Dense, overlapping rising tones from the magnetosphere above Alaska.

sources.title: OMEGA navigation tones
sources.geoNote: Marker shows where it was recorded.
sources.credit: Stephen P. McGreevy, Auroral Chorus II
sources.blurb: OMEGA was a worldwide very-low-frequency navigation network run under US leadership for ships and aircraft until it was switched off in 1997, superseded by GPS. Its stations took turns sending precisely timed tones.
sources.hear: Pulsed OMEGA tones alongside 'tweeks' from lightning, slightly slowed by the recordist.

sources.title: Voyager 1 at Jupiter's bow shock
sources.blurb: As Voyager 1 approached Jupiter in 1979 its plasma wave instrument crossed the bow shock, where the solar wind slams into the planet's magnetic field. NASA converted the data to audio.
sources.hear: The roar of charged particles at the edge of Jupiter's magnetosphere.
